question.text: Navratna Venture Fund (Cat I AIF) has three LPs: (i) Mr. Arjun Kapoor (resident individual, 40% units), (ii) Narayan Family Trust (resident, 35% units), (iii) Skyline Pension Fund BV (Netherlands-resident, 25% units). The fund distributes INR 20 crore of LTCG on unlisted shares (post-23-07-2024, non-business). What LTCG is allocated to the Dutch pension fund for its Indian tax return?

answer.text: Nil — non-resident LPs are exempt under Section 10(23FBA).
INR 20 crore — the full amount, because the fund is the legal seller.
INR 1.67 crore — split equally across the three LPs.
INR 5 crore — its 25% pro-rata share, retaining character as LTCG on unlisted shares.

explanation.text: The Logic: Under Section 115UB(1), the character AND proportion of income flowing through to each unitholder mirrors what they would have earned had they invested directly. Skyline Pension's allocation = 25% x 20 crore = INR 5 crore, taxable as LTCG on unlisted shares at 12.5% in India (subject to India-Netherlands DTAA for capital gains, if applicable). The other LPs get INR 8 crore and INR 7 crore respectively. The Trap: Option A wrongly exempts non-residents — the pass-through flows to all LPs; only treaty benefits (where available) can reduce tax. Option C ignores pass-through entirely. Option D wrongly splits equally rather than pro-rata to unit holding — the fund is not an equal-share partnership. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-C tests the same pro-rata allocation mechanics. The India-Netherlands treaty capital-gains article is a classic exam distractor — some treaties (like Mauritius pre-2016) used to exempt CG, but most modern treaties (including NL's) allow source-state taxation. XIX-E covers similar for Cat III. Manager's Pro-Tip: Build your fund-accounting LP schedule as a 'tax waterfall' — total income by character, pro-rata allocation to each LP based on COMMITTED units (not drawn), equalisation for late-closers. Auditors scrutinise this; an incorrect allocation key can trigger reassessment for the whole fund.
